newsitem.title: USA: Busy dlr hears hallelujah, quells FX trader blues.
newsitem.headline: Busy dlr hears hallelujah, quells FX trader blues.

text.p: Spectacular dollar moves in 1997 have lifted spirits among players in the U.S. foreign exchange market, displacing a lengthy bout of melancholy over corporate downsizing and a lack of gainful volatility.
Despite some hair-raising exchange rate swings in recent months, few traders were issuing their traditional jeremiads about thin summer markets.
Trading action attached to the dollar's advance to and selloff from an eight-year high against the mark this month has beefed up profits and contributed to a more sanguine industry outlook.

"The volatility we've seen this summer is kind of a bonus for us," said Kevin Lawrie, global manager of foreign exchange at Mellon Bank. "For the most part you can equate volatility with revenue; it's a positive correlation."
The revenue numbers reported by some of the large trading firms support the rosy outlook.
Trading profits at foreign exchange behemoth Citicorp, rose to $290 million in the second quarter from $225 million a year earlier and $260 million in the first quarter.

Renewed emphasis on the currency business by regional player BankBoston Corp was rewarded with a 67-percent jump in net forex earnings between the second quarters of 1996 and 1997. The firm also said it benefitted from higher profits from Asian operations, underscoring an important market trend.

Total foreign exchange volume, which stood at almost $1.3 trillion per day in 1995, has been growing strongly enough to quell fears of a sharp dropoff after Europe moves to a single currency. Turnover has been growing at an average annual clip of nearly 15 percent in recent years.

But Marc Chandler, a senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said volume was picking up mostly in emerging market currencies, for instance in Southeast Asia, at the expense of trading in Europe's Exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
"ERM desks are already lightening up and redeploying those forces elsewhere. You are going to see, I think, continued reduction in headcount," he said.

But many dealers now see a silver lining in the cloud of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU); they are dreading less the day the continent's many currencies merge into one, depriving some of a lucrative living.

The odds are high that "good" volatility will increase as EMU approaches, dealers said. Trading firms should continue to cash in on two-way action of the type experienced this year, which offered succor to day traders and trend followers alike.

The debate over which countries are in EMU and which are out at the start, planned for 1999, should continue to roil the markets, as will periodic rumors the entire scheme will be abandoned or postponed, dealers said.

"All this is going to contribute to volatiilty and the more divergent the major world economies are, and as they stand now Germany, Japan and the United States are divergent, the more volatile it's going to get." said Ben Strauss, a vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer.
"As far as the people in foreign exchange, it really couldn't be a better situation."
Foreign exchange traders are enjoying the best environment to practice their craft since the European Monetary System nearly shook apart in 1992 and 1993, Strauss said.
Improved technology has benefitted the strong niche players by cutting the pricing advantange of large banks and undermined their advantage in the quality of customer service, dealers said.

"It's kind of a level playing field now," said Mellon Bank's Lawrie. "For instance, a large regional will have the same price discovery as a major New York bank would have, through this electronic brokering system and technolgical efficiencies in the market. Therefore, we are just as competitive quoting the clients as they are."
